candidates.speaker: Jimmy Akin
candidates.proposition: Historical reliability should be assessed by verifying many major, intermediate, and lesser claims, not by demanding inerrancy or an unverifiable accuracy percentage.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted first-person presentation continues Jimmy Akin's identified opening statement and develops his announced reliability standard.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies the governing criterion by which Akin evaluates the Gospels and weighs verified claims against alleged errors throughout the debate.
candidates.contextSummary: After distinguishing reliability from inerrancy, Akin rejects percentage thresholds and proposes a tiered, cumulative test based on verified claims unless counterbalancing errors emerge.

candidates.speaker: Jimmy Akin
candidates.proposition: The Gospels accurately report major facts about Jesus, including his existence, Jewish identity, teaching, disciples, crucifixion, and condemnation by Pontius Pilate.
candidates.attributionBasis: Jimmy Akin explicitly presents his list and repeatedly identifies Bart Ehrman's stated agreement with these major historical claims.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Agreement on the principal outline of Jesus' life is Akin's first major application of his reliability criterion and directly supports the motion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's earlier position that the canonical Gospels are historically unreliable despite preserving some facts about Jesus.

candidates.contextSummary: Akin enumerates the Gospels' principal claims about Jesus and argues that even Ehrman's historical conclusions affirm the accuracy of this central narrative framework.

candidates.speaker: Jimmy Akin
candidates.proposition: Numerous intermediate Gospel claims about Jesus' chronology, origins, baptism, teachings, ministry, betrayal, trial, and crucifixion are also historically accurate.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same uninterrupted Akin presentation methodically attributes agreement on each intermediate claim to Bart Ehrman's published historical views.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The breadth of claimed agreement beyond a minimal outline is necessary to Akin's cumulative case that Gospel reliability is substantial rather than superficial.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's earlier contention that broad agreement on Jesus' existence and death does not make the Gospel narratives historically reliable.

candidates.contextSummary: Akin moves from major claims to a detailed set of intermediate propositions and argues that Ehrman accepts the Gospels as probably correct on all of them.

candidates.speaker: Jimmy Akin
candidates.proposition: The Gospels preserve many accurate lesser details, and the alleged errors presented do not counterbalance the cumulative accuracy of their major, intermediate, and minor claims.
candidates.attributionBasis: Akin continues the structured major-intermediate-lesser inventory and closes with an explicit first-person conclusion about historical reliability.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This completes the cumulative argument and expressly infers the debated conclusion after comparing the breadth of accepted material with the alleged discrepancies.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's earlier reliance on Gospel discrepancies to conclude that the documents are historically unreliable as narrative sources.

candidates.contextSummary: Akin catalogs accepted details about Jesus' practices, sayings, relationships, Jerusalem visit, trial, and Judas, then argues that the few alleged errors lack enough weight to overturn the larger pattern.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: Agreement on many general facts does not establish Gospel reliability because contradictions concerning the virgin birth, resurrection, and Jesus' self-presentation concern major claims.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Bart Ehrman's rebuttal immediately beforehand, and the speaker directly addresses Jimmy Akin by name and summarizes Akin's argument.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Ehrman directly rejects Akin's proposed inference from cumulative agreement to reliability and disputes the classification of the contradictions as merely minor.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Akin's position that agreement on many major, intermediate, and lesser claims establishes reliability unless alleged errors carry comparable cumulative weight.

candidates.contextSummary: Ehrman concedes the accepted facts but denies the resulting reliability judgment, labels the disputed theological narratives major, and uses an error-filled description of New York to challenge Akin's criterion.

candidates.speaker: Bart Ehrman
candidates.proposition: Mark and Luke present materially different theological portraits of Jesus' death, and harmonizing all four accounts erases each evangelist's intended message rather than vindicating their historical reliability.
candidates.attributionBasis: Bart Ehrman's uninterrupted rebuttal contrasts Mark and Luke in detail and repeatedly states his interpretive conclusion in the first person.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The extended comparison provides Ehrman's principal concrete demonstration that Gospel differences affect central portrayals and cannot be dismissed as incidental details.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Akin's position that Gospel differences are lesser matters compatible with a shared accurate account of Jesus' crucifixion and resurrection.

candidates.contextSummary: Ehrman contrasts Mark's despairing, largely silent Jesus with Luke's calm and informed Jesus, then argues that combining their sayings creates a synthetic account that obscures both authors' messages.

candidates.speaker: Jimmy Akin
candidates.proposition: Matthew and Luke agree on the virgin birth and all four Gospels agree on the resurrection, so disagreements about surrounding details do not negate those major claims.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator identifies Jimmy Akin's rebuttal, after which Akin explicitly recounts Bart Ehrman's objections and answers them directly.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly contests Ehrman's classification of the disputed material and preserves Akin's distinction between shared major claims and variable lesser details.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's rebuttal claim that disagreements in the birth and resurrection narratives concern major claims and undermine Gospel reliability.

candidates.contextSummary: Akin responds that Ehrman has conflated disagreement over narrative details with disagreement over the central events, which the relevant Gospels affirm in common.

candidates.speaker: Jimmy Akin
candidates.proposition: Ancient authors legitimately selected details and paraphrased speech, so omission of participants or variation in wording need not constitute historical contradiction.
candidates.attributionBasis: Jimmy Akin introduces named ancient writing practices, supplies his own examples, and directly solicits Bart Ehrman's agreement about selection.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Selection and paraphrase provide concrete interpretive mechanisms by which commonly alleged narrative discrepancies can coexist with accurate historical reporting.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's position that divergent Gospel details and expressions should count as contradictions that undermine the narratives' historical reliability.

candidates.contextSummary: Akin explains selection through the one-versus-two blind-men accounts and paraphrase through equivalent reports in different words, arguing that neither practice entails factual error.

candidates.speaker: Jimmy Akin
candidates.proposition: Ancient biographers could arrange events topically rather than chronologically, so differences in Gospel sequence may reflect literary organization instead of factual error.
candidates.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted Akin rebuttal explicitly introduces sequencing as another ancient practice and compares Suetonius, Mark, and Matthew.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The sequencing principle supplies a historically grounded answer to chronological discrepancies that otherwise contribute to the case against Gospel accuracy.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's position that differing arrangements and narrative presentations among the Gospels are evidence against their historical reliability.

candidates.contextSummary: Akin illustrates topical ordering with Suetonius and Matthew's grouping of the fig-tree episodes, arguing that awareness of such conventions resolves many apparent discrepancies.

candidates.speaker: Jimmy Akin
candidates.proposition: Ancient Gospel accounts ordinarily convey an accurate gist with approximate details, and evaluating them as if they promised modern precision mistakes their intended level of reporting.
candidates.attributionBasis: Jimmy Akin continues his rebuttal with an extended approximation analogy and explicitly applies the resulting gist principle to the evangelists.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The gist principle gives Akin a broad methodological defense of variable details while retaining the historical accuracy of the narratives' essential content.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Ehrman's position that differences in Gospel details and wording amount to errors sufficient to characterize the narratives as historically unreliable.

candidates.contextSummary: Using differing but compatible estimates of an arrival time, Akin argues that ancient audiences expected approximate accounts and that pressing their details beyond intended precision generates false contradictions.
